item.title: A Chinese Robot Beat Usain Bolt’s 100-Meter Record. Should We Be Impressed?
item.description:
In 2009, Usain Bolt set the men’s 100-meter dash world record of 9.58 seconds at the World Athletics Championships in Berlin. On Saturday, a humanoid robot developed by the Chinese company X-Humanoid beat that record by 0.19 seconds, according to Chinese state media. The robot ended its sprint by slamming full speed into a padded wall, falling down and being carried away by human assistants.

High-profile feats of robotic athleticism have become increasingly common in China, where a humanoid robotics industry has flourished, aided by generous state support and billions in investment. Robots have danced and performed martial arts at the country’s top events.

At the World Humanoid Robot Games in Beijing over the weekend, they boxed and participated in soccer matches. One played tennis against a human opponent, moving across the court and angling itself to return volleys. Earlier this year, a robot ran a marathon faster than any human in history.

But what do these robotic superhuman feats amount to?

“Most of the sports the humanoids are doing don’t directly translate into utility for many of the mundane tasks people are trying to get humanoids to perform, like being useful around the house,” said Michael Milford, a professor and director of the robotics center at Queensland University of Technology in Australia.

The robots are “capable in very specific and somewhat contrived events,” he said.

Chinese media has also acknowledged the gulf between athleticism and real-world applications in its coverage of the games.

“A factory robot does not need to win a sprint, nor does a service robot need a medal,” read a commentary in Xinhua, the state news agency. “But every gain in speed, stability and precision on the competition floor can bring robots one step closer to becoming genuinely useful beyond it.”

Even without significant and proven real-world applications, these high-profile displays and the attention they have attracted are already paying some dividends. Unitree Robotics — a humanoid robotics company whose videos of robots performing kung fu, kickboxing and back flips have attracted millions of views online, and whose robots featured heavily at the Humanoid Robot Games last year — debuted on the Shanghai stock market last week. Its shares ended their first day of trading up by more than 460 percent.

Alan Fern, a robotics professor at Oregon State University, was part of a research team that set the Guinness World Record for the fastest 100-meter run by a robot on two legs in 2022. That robot ran it in 24.73 seconds. To go from that, in four years, to X-Humanoid’s 9.39 seconds was an “enormous achievement,” he said.

But he noted that robotics companies have become relatively experienced in making robots that can run, jump and do acrobatics in controlled environments. He added that incremental improvements in these sports are mostly related to developing better hardware and refining the controls, rather than any significant technological breakthrough.

The robot at the games in Beijing that could play tennis against a human was more impressive, he said, because that involved interacting with something unpredictable.

Most robots struggle in situations where they need to adapt to changing situations. Yet the tennis robot had to track a fast-moving ball, decide where to move, coordinate its body and time the strike.

The robots are still far from perfect, with accidents abounding at the games. Robots fell down, sparked small fires and crashed into objects, according to videos of the event. The unusual running style of one machine, with its arms up near its face, earned it the nickname “shy robot” on the social media platform Weibo. Many of the racing robots did not seem capable of slowing down on their own and instead stopped by running into a padded barrier.

The vision of humanoid robots eventually being able to do anything a human can do is still far away, Mr. Fern said.

“Outside entertainment and a limited number of tightly constrained industrial settings, these robots do not yet have the general-purpose intelligence and reliability needed to operate in messy real-world environments,” he said.

Mr. Milford said that it could take many years before robots can safely and reliably perform in everyday settings.

He drew a comparison to self-driving cars: Three or four decades ago, a self-driving car could drive across a continent on highways. But only in recent years has the technology become advanced and safe enough for such cars to be deployed widely and largely without incident.

Car racing may be another good analogy, Mr. Fern said. “We still marvel at the engineering achievements in Formula 1, and some of those advances eventually transfer elsewhere, but we do not interpret every faster lap as a revolution in transportation,” he said.

“Similarly, beating Usain Bolt does not mean that the robot has surpassed humans at locomotion in any general sense,” he added.

Mr. Bolt did not respond to a request for comment.

Siyi Zhaocontributed research.

item.title: Christian Convert Who Fled Iran and Was Ousted From U.S. Finds a New Home
item.description:
The young woman became the face of migrants deported by the United States to Panama. She was locked up in a hotel, detained in a camp in the Darién jungle and stranded in a country where she knew neither the language nor anyone else. Later, she lent her name to a bill in Congress aimed at providing more protection to some migrants seeking asylum in the United States.

The woman, Artemis Ghasemzadeh, a 28-year-old Iranian Christian convert, has now found a home — in Canada. In June, the Canadian government granted her asylum, a happy bookend to her nearly two-year journey fleeing religious persecution in Iran only to get entangled in the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown.

Ms. Ghasemzadeh arrived on Denman Island near Vancouver in early July with few belongings other than clothes. But her heart, she said, was filled with gratitude and hope for a new beginning.

“I’m still kind of in shock. I can’t believe I’m really here and this is not a dream,” Ms. Ghasemzadeh said in a telephone interview. “I can finally say the struggle is over.”

Ms. Ghasemzadeh left Iran for Mexico in December 2024 with her brother, Shahin, also a Christian covert, and entered the United States by jumping over a wall on the southern border. Border patrol officers caught and transferred them to detention facilities, separating them. In February 2025, she was shackled and put on a U.S. military plane heading to Panama.

That flight was the Trump administration’s first experiment with deporting migrants to a third country, meaning a place where they are not citizens. Since then, third-country flights have gone to at least 18 countries including Costa Rica, El Salvador and the Central African Republic, among others. The Trump administration, despite its acute hostility toward Iran’s government, has nonetheless worked with it to send at least two deportation flights directly to Iran.

For Ms. Ghasemzadeh, the prospect of being sent back to Iran was terrifying. Iran’s law considers leaving Islam for another faith as blasphemy, punishable by death. Christians born to the faith are free to practice but converts attend secret underground churches and prayer groups to evade arrest and persecution.

“I wanted to live freely, to live without fear, to live without someone wanting to kill me,” Ms. Ghasemzadeh said in an interview in 2025.

After Ms. Ghasemzadeh and her fellow deportees were flown out of the United States, Panama had locked them in a hotel in Panama City and later transported them in the middle of the night to a migrant detention camp in the Darién jungle, where they were held for weeks.

Ms Ghasemzadeh had a singular role in drawing the world’s attention to their plight. She made a social media video that went viral and with her smuggled cellphone provided updates to The New York Times. The coverage gained wide attention, including from Christian advocacy organizations and rights activists. A group of high-profile immigration lawyers took on the case pro bono and won the deportees’ release from jungle detention.

Panama, facing lawsuits and an international uproar, granted the deportees a 90-day humanitarian visa. Many eventually left Panama, but Ms. Ghasemzadeh decided to stay and search for a legal path to North America. She hoped to be reunited with her brother, who was granted asylum in the United States this year and now lives in Texas.

In May 2025, Representative Yassamin Ansari, a Democrat from Arizona who is Iranian American, introduced legislation in Congress called the Artemis Act. The bill sought to prohibit the expedited removal of individuals fleeing countries that the State Department says persecute religious minorities and to ensure they have the chance to claim asylum in a U.S. immigration court. The legislation had widespread support from Democrats but faced opposition from Republicans, who hold the majority in the House.

Lawyers said they told Ms. Ghasemzadeh that the chances of the United States reversing its decision and allowing her back were slim given the political climate around the immigration issue.

Immigrating to Canada presented its own challenges. The country had a quota for refugees and required a Canadian citizen to sponsor their applications. She did not know anyone in Canada.

Meanwhile, Ms. Ghasemzadeh said, she tried to build a life in Panama City. She found a church, learned Spanish, made friends and worked as a dental hygienist.

In Canada, Ian and Naomi Elliot, a retired couple who run programs for their local Afghan refugee community, read a profile of Ms. Ghasemzadeh in The Times anddecided to sponsor her asylum application. The couple said they had helped an Afghan and an Ethiopian secure asylum in Canada.

“I couldn’t sleep after reading the article. I thought this is a Christian sister who shares our faith and is paying a massive price for this belief,” said Mr. Elliot, 68, who works with InterVarsity Christian Fellowship and is a community leader at their small church on Denman Island.

The Elliots undertook a monthslong effort, contacting Canadian officials, refugee aid agencies and activists, while consulting lawyers in three different countries. The couple prayed for her every night. But “everywhere we tried, the door was shut,” said Mr. Elliot, because Canada’s quota for privately sponsored refugees in 2025 had been filled and there was a long waiting list.

Then shortly before Christmas, they said, they received an unexpected call. City of Refugees, an agency that facilitates the resettlement of persecuted Christians in Canada, called Mr. Elliot. The agency had a cancellation and would give the spot to Ms. Ghasemzadeh.

The agency gave Mr. Elliot 48 hours to submit her paperwork, find a church to sponsor her and put up $25,000. The first two tasks were easy, but coming up with the money on short notice was difficult. He called an American lawyer in Texas who had helped Ms. Ghasemzadeh’s brother, and although the two had never met, the lawyer wired money to Mr. Elliot’s bank account.

Ms. Ghasemzadeh had only a few days to get ready for her departure, she said.

“The first thing I thought was that I don’t have to worry about getting displaced again,” she recalled. “I can finally get my own place and not live in shelters. I want to go to university and study dental hygiene or dentistry, and then travel freely without fear.”

In Canada, the Elliots were preparing for her arrival, outfitting her future bedroom with a desk, chair, mirror and a green plant, as well as new sheets and curtains. They also bought her a bathing suit, which she would need for summering on the island.

“Big hearts make a huge difference. It all worked out like a miracle,” said Naomi Elliot, 65, who said her parents and grandparents survived the Holocaust in Europe and later migrated to Canada.

On the day of her arrival, Mr. Elliot and his friends drove excitedly to the nearby airport, while Ms. Elliot stayed home to prepare a lunch feast. They brought flowers, gifts and signs that said “Welcome Artemis” in English and Persian.

When she arrived, Ms. Ghasemzadeh ran to Mr. Elliot and hugged him tightly. “Thank you for saving my life,” she told him. They both cried.
